outline: 1942 Permutations involving Grouping, Complements, and Cases

examples.question_text: A badminton squad has $11$ players. In how many ways can $3$ players be selected for a team if positions do not matter?
examples.solution_text:
Order does not matter, so choose $3$ players from $11$.
$\begin{align*}{}^{11}C_{3}&=\frac{11!}{3!8!}\\&=\frac{11\times10\times9}{3\times2\times1}\\&=165\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A committee needs $2$ Physics teachers, $3$ Maths teachers and $1$ English teacher. There are $6$ Physics teachers, $7$ Maths teachers and $4$ English teachers available. How many committees can be formed?
examples.solution_text:
Choose the required teachers from each subject, then multiply the selection counts.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}{}^{6}C_{2}\times{}^{7}C_{3}\times{}^{4}C_{1}\\&=15\times35\times4\\&=2100\end{align*}$

(a) Each pair determines one line.
$\begin{align*}{}^{6}C_{2}&=\frac{6\times5}{2\times1}\\&=15\end{align*}$
(b) No three points on a circle are collinear, so each triple determines one triangle.
$\begin{align*}{}^{6}C_{3}&=\frac{6\times5\times4}{3\times2\times1}\\&=20\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A coin is tossed $7$ times. How many sequences contain exactly $3$ heads?
examples.solution_text:
Choose $3$ of the $7$ positions for heads. The remaining positions must be tails.
$\begin{align*}{}^{7}C_{3}&=\frac{7!}{3!4!}\\&=\frac{7\times6\times5}{3\times2\times1}\\&=35\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A team of $4$ players is selected from a squad of $10$. How many teams can be chosen if the captain must be included?
examples.solution_text:
Include the captain, then choose $3$ players from the $9$ remaining.
$\begin{align*}{}^{9}C_{3}&=\frac{9!}{3!6!}\\&=\frac{9\times8\times7}{3\times2\times1}\\&=84\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A committee of $4$ people is selected from $12$ members. How many committees can be formed if one particular member must be excluded?
examples.solution_text:
Exclude that member, then choose $4$ people from the $11$ remaining.
$\begin{align*}{}^{11}C_{4}&=\frac{11!}{4!7!}\\&=\frac{11\times10\times9\times8}{4\times3\times2\times1}\\&=330\end{align*}$

examples.derivation: An unordered team requires choosing three players: 11C3 = (11 × 10 × 9)/6 = 165.
The subject groups are disjoint. Their selection counts multiply: 6C2 × 7C3 × 4C1 = 15 × 35 × 4 = 2100.

The diagram contains six distinct labelled points on one circle. Each pair determines a distinct line, giving 6C2 = 15. No line intersects a circle in three distinct points, so every triple forms a triangle: 6C3 = 20.
Choosing the three head positions uniquely determines the sequence: 7C3 = (7 × 6 × 5)/6 = 35.
Including the captain fills one of four places and leaves nine eligible players: 9C3 = (9 × 8 × 7)/6 = 84.
Excluding the specified member leaves eleven eligible members while four places remain: 11C4 = (11 × 10 × 9 × 8)/24 = 330.
